title: Beta Radiation in Nuclear Physics
short_intro: Beta radiation consists of high-speed electrons (beta-minus) or positrons (beta-plus) emitted from atomic nuclei during radioactive decay. This process involves the weak nuclear force, which transforms a neutron into a proton or vice versa, thereby changing the atomic number by one while keeping the mass number constant.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic types of beta decay (beta-minus and beta-plus), conservation laws in beta decay, properties of beta particles, and neutrino hypothesis.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Fermi's theory of beta decay, continuous beta spectrum analysis, Kurie plots, parity non-conservation in weak interactions, and orbital electron capture.

prerequisites: Conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum
Pauli's exclusion principle and neutrino concept

concept_notes.heading: Types of Beta Decay
bullets: Beta-minus decay occurs when an unstable neutron-rich nucleus emits an electron and an electron antineutrino, converting a neutron into a proton: n → p + e&sup- + ν̄<sub>e</sub>.
Beta-plus decay occurs in proton-rich nuclei where a proton converts into a neutron, emitting a positron and an electron neutrino: p → n + e&sup+ + ν<sub>e</sub>.

Electron capture is a competing process where an inner-shell electron (typically K-shell) is captured by the nucleus, converting a proton into a neutron and emitting a neutrino: p + e&sup- → n + ν<sub>e</sub>.

concept_notes.heading: Continuous Beta Spectrum and the Neutrino
bullets: Unlike alpha decay, which exhibits discrete energy lines, beta decay yields a continuous energy spectrum of emitted electrons ranging from zero up to a maximum kinetic energy (E<sub>max</sub>).
To preserve the conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum (spin 1/2), Wolfgang Pauli postulated the existence of a neutral, nearly massless spin-1/2 particle called the neutrino.
The available decay energy Q is shared continuously between the beta particle, the recoiling daughter nucleus, and the neutrino (or antineutrino).

concept_notes.heading: Energetics of Beta Decay
bullets: For beta-minus decay to occur spontaneously, the mass of the parent neutral atom must exceed the mass of the daughter neutral atom: M(Z, A) > M(Z+1, A).
For beta-plus decay, the mass of the parent neutral atom must exceed the mass of the daughter atom by at least two electron masses: M(Z, A) > M(Z-1, A) + 2m<sub>e</sub>c².
For electron capture, the mass condition is simply M(Z, A) > M(Z-1, A) (neglecting binding energy of the captured electron).

concept_notes.heading: Fermi's Theory of Beta Decay
bullets: Enrico Fermi formulated a quantitative theory of beta decay modeled after quantum electrodynamics, treating the beta particle and neutrino as being created at the moment of emission.

The transition rate (decay probability per unit time) is governed by Fermi's Golden Rule, proportional to the square of the matrix element of the weak interaction and the density of final states (phase space factor).
The shape of the allowed beta spectrum is explicitly derived by integrating over the available momenta of the electron and neutrino.

derivations.title: Kinematic Q-Value for Beta-Minus Decay
derivations.conditions: Rest frame of the parent nucleus, utilizing atomic masses to account for orbital electrons.
steps: Write the nuclear mass conservation equation for parent mass M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z, A) decaying to daughter nuclear mass M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z+1, A) plus electron mass m<sub>e</sub> and neutrino mass m<sub>ν</sub> ≈ 0.
Q = [M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z, A) - M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z+1, A) - m<sub>e</sub>] c².
Add Z electron masses m<sub>e</sub> to both parent and daughter nuclear masses to convert them into neutral atomic masses M(Z, A) and M(Z+1, A).
Q = [M(Z, A) - Z m<sub>e</sub> - (M(Z+1, A) - (Z+1) m<sub>e</sub>) - m<sub>e</sub>] c².
Simplify the electron mass terms: Z m<sub>e</sub> - (Z + 1) m<sub>e</sub> + m<sub>e</sub> = 0.

derivations.title: Kinematic Q-Value for Beta-Plus Decay
derivations.conditions: Rest frame of the parent nucleus, accounting for positron emission and atomic electron balance.
steps: Write the nuclear mass conservation equation for positron decay: M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z, A) → M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z-1, A) + m<sub>e</sub> + m<sub>ν</sub>.
Q = [M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z, A) - M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z-1, A) - m<sub>e</sub>] c².
Convert nuclear masses to neutral atomic masses by adding Z electron masses to the parent and (Z-1) electron masses to the daughter.
M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z, A) = M(Z, A) - Z m<sub>e</sub> and M<sub>nuc</sub>(Z-1, A) = M(Z-1, A) - (Z-1) m<sub>e</sub>.
Substitute these into the Q-value equation: Q = [M(Z, A) - Z m<sub>e</sub> - (M(Z-1, A) - (Z-1) m<sub>e</sub>) - m<sub>e</sub>] c².
Combine the electron mass terms: -Z m<sub>e</sub> + (Z-1) m<sub>e</sub> - m<sub>e</sub> = -2 m<sub>e</sub>.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Beta Decay Energy Spectrum
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of number of emitted beta particles N(E) versus kinetic energy E, showing a continuous curve rising from zero, peaking around 1/3 to 1/2 of E<sub>max</sub>, and dropping sharply to zero at E = E<sub>max</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that beta particles are emitted with a continuous distribution of energies, proving the existence of a third unseen particle (the neutrino) sharing the decay energy.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested to contrast with discrete alpha and gamma spectra.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kurie Plot
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight line plot of [N(E)/F(Z,E)pE]<sup>1/2</sup> against kinetic energy E, intersecting the energy axis at E = Q.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Linearizes the beta spectrum data, confirming Fermi's theory and allowing an accurate determination of the maximum endpoint energy Q (and upper limit of neutrino mass).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT exams regarding graphical verification of Fermi theory and endpoint energy determination.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Absorption of Beta Radiation by Matter
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A semi-logarithmic plot of transmitted beta intensity versus absorber thickness (e.g., aluminum foil), showing an initial near-exponential decrease followed by a tail due to Bremsstrahlung X-rays.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Beta particles have a well-defined maximum range in matter due to continuous ionization energy losses, unlike gamma rays which exhibit pure exponential attenuation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Distinguishing the interaction mechanisms of alpha, beta, and gamma radiations.

solved_numericals.question: In a beta-minus decay, if the mass of the parent atom <sup>24</sup>Na is 23.990963 u and the mass of the daughter atom <sup>24</sup>Mg is 23.985042 u, calculate the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted beta particle in MeV. (1 u = 931.5 MeV/c²)
solution_steps: Identify the Q-value formula for beta-minus decay: Q = [M(Z, A) - M(Z+1, A)] c².
Substitute the given atomic masses: Q = (23.990963 u - 23.985042 u) c².
Convert mass difference to energy: Q = 0.005921 × 931.5 MeV = 5.515 MeV.

solved_numericals.question: Determine the threshold atomic mass difference for a nucleus to undergo spontaneous positron (beta-plus) decay, and calculate the minimum mass excess required for <sup>11</sup>C (atomic mass 11.011434 u) to decay to <sup>11</sup>B (atomic mass 11.009305 u). Given m<sub>e</sub> = 0.0005486 u.
solution_steps: Write the Q-value condition for beta-plus decay: Q = [M(Z, A) - M(Z-1, A) - 2m_e] c² > 0.
Condition for spontaneous decay: M(Z, A) > M(Z-1, A) + 2m_e.
Substitute the atomic masses for <sup>11</sup>C and <sup>11</sup>B: M(C-11) = 11.011434 u, M(B-11) = 11.009305 u.
Compare parent mass: 11.011434 u > 11.0104022 u, hence decay is energetically allowed.

solved_numericals.question: A radioactive sample undergoes beta-minus decay with a half-life of 14.3 days. Calculate the decay constant λ and the time required for 75% of the initial nuclei to decay.
solution_steps: Use the half-life relation: T<sub>1/2</sub> = ln(2) / λ.
If 75% of the nuclei have decayed, the remaining fraction is N(t) / N<sub>0</sub> = 1 - 0.75 = 0.25 = (1/4).
Apply the radioactive decay law: N(t) = N_0 e^{-\lambda t} ⇒ 0.25 = e^{-\lambda t}.
Take natural logarithm on both sides: ln(0.25) = -λ t ⇒ -1.3863 = -0.04846 t.
Solve for t: t = 1.3863 / 0.04846 = 28.6 days (which is exactly 2 half-lives).

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: The neutrino mass is treated as zero or extremely small in standard non-relativistic Q-value calculations. Limitation: Precise measurements of beta spectra near the endpoint require non-zero neutrino mass corrections.

Assumption: Orbital electron binding energies are neglected in crude Q-value estimates. Limitation: Binding energy becomes critical when calculating accurate threshold energies for electron capture and low-energy beta transitions.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Beta particles are orbital electrons emitted from the atom.
common_misconceptions.correct: Beta particles are created within and emitted from the atomic nucleus via the conversion of a neutron into a proton (or vice versa).
common_misconceptions.why: Orbital electrons do not have sufficient energy nor do they originate from nuclear transitions; the weak force governs beta decay.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Beta decay has a sharp, discrete energy spectrum similar to alpha decay.
common_misconceptions.correct: Beta decay produces a continuous energy spectrum.
common_misconceptions.why: The available decay energy is shared dynamically between the beta particle, the recoiling nucleus, and an undetected neutrino.

common_misconceptions.wrong: A free neutron decays into a proton without emitting any other particle.
common_misconceptions.correct: A free neutron decays into a proton, an electron, and an electron antineutrino.
common_misconceptions.why: Lepton number, angular momentum, and energy conservation require the emission of an antineutrino.

quick_revision: Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton: n → p + e&sup- + ν̄<sub>e</sub>.
Beta-plus decay converts a proton into a neutron: p → n + e&sup+ + ν<sub>e</sub>.
Electron capture involves a nucleus absorbing an inner-shell electron: p + e&sup- → n + ν<sub>e</sub>.
The continuous beta energy spectrum led Pauli to postulate the neutrino.
Beta-minus Q-value condition: M(Z, A) > M(Z+1, A).
Beta-plus Q-value condition: M(Z, A) > M(Z-1, A) + 2m<sub>e</sub>.
Kurie plots linearize the beta spectrum to find the endpoint energy Q.
Fermi's theory successfully explains the transition probabilities of allowed beta decays.
